title: Quantum Meta-Complexity Is All You Need: Characterizing One-Way Puzzles via Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity
abstract: We initiate the time-bounded meta-complexity program for quantum cryptography. Recent work characterizes one-way puzzles, the minimal search primitive of quantum cryptography without one-way functions, by the average-case hardness of approximating the plain, uncomputable Kolmogorov complexity over quantumly samplable distributions; the classical program of Liu and Pass, by contrast, lives at polynomial time bounds. We define a probabilistic time-bounded quantum program complexity pKq^t for classical strings and prove two unconditional theorems. First, a quantum coding theorem: any string output by a quantum polynomial-time sampler with probability delta admits a description of the information-theoretically optimal length log(1/delta) plus logarithmic terms, decodable by a quantum machine in time O(sqrt(1/delta)) times a polynomial, via amplitude amplification over the coherently executed sampler. Second, an exact characterization at subexponential time: one-way puzzles exist if and only if the gap problem for pKq at time bound 2^(n/2) poly(n) is weakly quantum-average-hard, refining the plain-complexity characterizations. We then isolate the polynomial-time coding theorem as the single load-bearing open conjecture of the program, prove that it implies the full polynomial-time characterization, analyze why the classical derandomization proof resists quantization, and formulate a relativized barrier conjecture delimiting string-valued meta-complexity at one-way puzzles. Conjectures are labeled as such throughout.
summary: This work develops a quantum meta-complexity framework to characterize one-way puzzles, proving that their existence is equivalent to a specific quantum average-case hardness problem. The authors establish a quantum coding theorem and highlight that string-based complexity is sufficient for puzzles but potentially insufficient for more complex quantum state generators.
main_problem: The paper aims to characterize the existence of one-way puzzles using time-bounded quantum meta-complexity, establishing a necessary and sufficient condition based on quantum average-case hardness.
main_result: It proves that one-way puzzles exist if and only if the gap problem for the quantum time-bounded complexity measure ($pKt_q$) is weakly quantum-average-hard at subexponential time bounds.
method: The methodology involves defining the probabilistic time-bounded quantum program complexity ($pKt_q$) and utilizing quantum coding theorems derived via amplitude amplification to link information-theoretic bounds to computational hardness.
model_or_system: The focus is on quantum computation models applied to classical strings, specifically analyzing one-way puzzles (minimal search primitives for quantum cryptography) and comparing them to one-way state generators.
key_observables: Probabilistic time-bounded quantum program complexity ($pKt_q$), sampling mass ($\delta$), and the hardness of the gap problem ($	ext{Gap-}pKt^*_q$).
important_parameters: Time bounds, particularly subexponential time $t^*(n) = 2n/2	ext{poly}(n)$, and the probability $\delta$ of the quantum sampler.
main_assumptions: The core results rely on several conjectures, notably the polynomial-time coding theorem (Conjecture 5.3), which remains unproven.
figures_summary: Figure 1 maps cryptographic primitives to complexity measures; Figure 3 shows the surprisal distribution for a random circuit sampler; Figure 4 validates the quantum decoder's scaling against theoretical bounds.
paper_structure: The paper develops the meta-complexity program by defining $pKt_q$, proving the quantum coding theorem (Theorem 5.1), establishing the main equivalence (Theorem 6.1), and concluding with open conjectures regarding state generators and the barrier conjecture.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, the rigorous connection between information-theoretic complexity measures (like Kolmogorov complexity) and the existence of cryptographic primitives provides deep theoretical insights into the limits of quantum computation.
